newsitem.title: UK: Oil market welcomes IPE move to enforce trading rules.
newsitem.headline: Oil market welcomes IPE move to enforce trading rules.

text.p: Oil market players have mostly welcomed a move by London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE) aimed at stamping out breaches in futures trading rules by fining a large brokerage and four of its traders.

They say the decision to make public details of the punishment of PVM Oil Futures Ltd and four of its traders for failing to execute unmatched client orders and cross trades is unusual and may signal a change of direction at the IPE which has tended to keep such action closely guarded.

The IPE, the world's second largest energy futures exchange, on Friday said PVM was fined 30,000 stg after it "accepted liability" for the actions of several of its floor trading team which broke IPE rules between October 30, 1995 and March 28, 1996.
The exchange said "possible irregularities" were identified as "a result of routine continuous surveillance."
"We are trying to enforce the rules more consistently, positively and transparently," said IPE Chief Executive Lynton Jones who took over his position last year.
A PVM spokesman declined to comment on the fines or the suspension for six months of one of its brokers but others said the fine would act as a deterrent to other floor traders.
Most traders expect little impact on volume at the IPE but some see traders shifting their orders towards other brokers.

"It probably won't hit the exchange but traders will continually monitor how their brokers perform," said Nigel Saperia, managing director of the oil division of Bankers Trust International in London.

Confidence among oil companies that orders will be executed according to the trading rules is critical to the exchange's success. But those same companies often take their own action if they feel the broker has not been working hard on their account.
"In the end traders will always tend to use the brokers they feel most comfortable with," said Scott Carter, senior trader, at Tosco Europe Ltd in London.
Traders say rules and regulation alone are not enough to ensure broker performance and irregularities occur in both futures and over-the-counter (OTC) markets.

Placing an order on the futures exchange floor should ensure it reaches the pit and is open for any participant to trade against. But OTC markets, are usually brokered on the telephone which inevitably sometimes mis-match bids and offers.
Despite that apparent disadvantage, OTC oil markets thrive partly because traders can keep a close watch on their deals.
Oil traders routinely stay on an open telephone line to their broker during the execution of an OTC deal, only yielding control to the broker at the very last minute.
By comparison, traders give IPE brokers more discretion by "leaving" orders for them to execute on the floor of the exchange.

After enjoying huge growth over the past 10 years, futures exchanges are facing growing pressure for change. OTC markets can offer traders a more flexible alternative to futures while computerised trading systems can sharply cut transaction costs.
But a senior IPE official sees no reason for the IPE to lose business to other oil derivatives markets.
"They are complementary because they mutually reinforce each other," said Trevor Christmas, senior vice president, marketing at the IPE.

To enhance their competitive edge, some commodities futures exchanges have merged to form mega-exchanges while others, including the IPE have linked up with other exchanges to launch contracts traded in more than one time zone.
The IPE has also invested in a computerised trading system on which it will launch a long awaited natural gas contract on Friday.
The IPE has been under the spotlight since launching a probe into a tussle between two oil trading houses on gas oil futures last November.

A shadow was cast over futures trading by the Sumitomo scandal at the London Metal Exchange last year and by the big Metallgeschellschaft AG losses three years ago on the New York Mercantile Exchange.
